tagline: The back road to Santa Fe, by the mining towns.
intro: From the Tijeras interchange on I-40, east of Albuquerque, NM 14 heads north through Cedar Crest into piñon and juniper hills. At San Antonito a spur, NM 536, climbs off to Sandia Crest. The main road goes on past the old gold camp of Golden, down into Madrid and through Los Cerrillos to Santa Fe, 52 miles that take only a little longer than the interstate.
The name comes from the turquoise of the Cerrillos Hills, which Ancestral Puebloans were mining by about 700 to 900 AD. The Spanish noted lead and silver there in 1581. Coal came after.

moments.title: Sandia Crest
moments.text: At the end of NM 536 the ridge tops out at 10,679 feet. On its west side the mountains fall more than 4,000 feet in two miles to Albuquerque.

moments.title: Golden
moments.text: Gold turned up here in 1825, years before California's rush. The 2020 census counted 19 residents, along with a general store open since 1918.

moments.title: Madrid
moments.text: A company coal town for 80 years and never incorporated, built from prefabricated miners' cabins shipped in by rail from as far as Topeka. Galleries line the highway now.
